item.title: New Venture Professionalization: Processes, Tradeoffs, and Performance Implications
item.content:encoded:
This special issue in the Journal of Business Venturing examines how new ventures undergo professionalization and the implications of this organizational development. The call seeks research exploring the processes through which entrepreneurial firms adopt more formal structures, systems, and practices, as well as the strategic tradeoffs involved in professionalization efforts and their effects on organizational performance.

item.title: Entrepreneurship and the Creation of Decent Work for All
item.content:encoded:
This multi-journal collection addresses the relationship between entrepreneurship and decent work, aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goal 8. The collection recognizes that recent disruptions have highlighted how rapidly employment situations can change, and that entrepreneurship may play a significant role in creating quality employment opportunities, particularly in volatile environments.

The collection seeks to bring together diverse research perspectives on how entrepreneurship can contribute to productive employment, fair wages, improved labor market access, and better job opportunities across different contexts and populations. Both research and review articles are welcome, and all submissions will undergo rigorous peer review according to each journal's standards.

Appel publié par Small Business Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Equal pay for work of equal value
  • Gender discrimination in employment
  • Immigration and employment
  • Labor shortages after COVID-19
  • Modern slavery and child labor
  • Labor policy
  • Entrepreneurial enterprises, SMEs, and family businesses
  • Global entrepreneurial firms: organization design, emerging conceptions in entrepreneurship (i.e. born globals), globalization's challenges and opportunities, cultural differences
  • Remote work
  • Opportunity entrepreneurship as a direct way to generate high quality employment
  • Measuring and dealing with positive and negative externalities of new businesses

item.title: Entrepreneurship, Creative Destruction, and Growth: Enriching the Aghion-Howitt Tradition
item.content:encoded:
Philippe Aghion, Collège de France

Martin Andersson, Blekinge Institute of Technology

David B. Audretsch, Indiana University

Maksim Belitski, University of Reading

Pontus Braunerhjelm, KTH Royal Institute of Technology

This special issue seeks to advance Schumpeterian research that integrates entrepreneurial activities across multiple levels of analysis. It focuses on connecting individual entrepreneurs and firms with regional innovation ecosystems and industrial dynamics, while also considering broader institutional and policy frameworks.

The issue welcomes research on the full lifecycle of ventures, including formation, growth, contraction, and failure, with particular emphasis on how these dynamics drive productivity improvements. It also invites studies that enrich the Aghion-Howitt growth model with contemporary entrepreneurship research insights.

Appel publié par Small Business Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • New venture formation and post-entry dynamics
  • Scaling, displacement, and exit in entrepreneurial firms
  • Reallocation dynamics and productivity growth
  • The Aghion-Howitt framework and entrepreneurship research
  • Multi-level analysis connecting micro (entrepreneurs and firms), meso (regional ecosystems and industrial structure), and macro (institutional configurations and policy regimes) levels
  • Innovation and its transformation into productivity growth within the Schumpeterian tradition

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Entrepreneurship Ex Machina: Transformative Artificial Intelligence for Theory and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Martin Obschonka, University of Amsterdam

Moren Lévesque, York University

Frédéric Ooms, HEC Liège

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Denis A. Grégoire, HEC Montréal

Tara S. Behrend, Michigan State University

Boris Nikolaev, Colorado State University

Transformative Artificial Intelligence (AI) — that is, the use of AI tools that have such inherent capabilities that they could induce societal transitions similar to that of the agricultural or industrial revolutions — has become an omnipresent topic of interest. Because these tools offer order-of-magnitude efficiency improvements over prior ways of performing various human tasks, important research opportunities arise for better understanding their transformative impact.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theorizing on algorithmic entrepreneurship
  • Mechanisms of external enablement of entrepreneurship via AI (e.g., generative AI)
  • Can AI help reduce the destructive aspects of entrepreneurship (e.g., societal and personal costs)?
  • Can AI create resource abundance, overcoming typical entrepreneurial resource scarcity and challenging leading startup methods (e.g., effectuation/bricolage, bootstrapping, lean startup)?
  • Do classic research findings and theories (e.g., on the role of knowledge and human and social capital in entrepreneurship) still hold in the new AI era?
  • How can AI impact entrepreneurial finance (e.g., AI-powered financial planning for entrepreneurs, VC investment portfolio management and decisions) and resource acquisition (e.g., entrepreneurs' pitch preparation, investors' due diligence, etc.)?
  • Does AI change the age curve associated with entrepreneurship (does it replace the advantage of industry experience, and do we therefore see an AI-empowered rise of youth entrepreneurs)?
  • How can AI contribute to equality and diversity (e.g., neurodiversity, closing the gender gap)?
  • Ethical and legal issues of algorithmic entrepreneurship and AI-supported research
  • How can AI support entrepreneurs' cognition, decision making, and psychological well-being?
  • Will the emerging AI economy of abundance replace entrepreneurship/human entrepreneurs?

Timeline

  • January 31, 2026: Final deadline for proposal submissions

item.title: Time in Entrepreneurship: New Perspectives and Approaches
item.content:encoded:
Ludvig Levasseur, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Moren Lévesque, York University

Paul Spee, University of Queensland

Ute Stephan, King's College London

Matthew Wood, University of Oklahoma

This special issue seeks manuscripts advancing our understanding of time in entrepreneurship. Research on the duration, pace, timing, and speed of action calibration in entrepreneurial processes such as opportunity realization are key examples of the role temporal dynamics play in entrepreneurship. Time is equally critical when examining decisions about the timing of growth while managing external events and shocks alongside slowly or rapidly evolving industry trends and customer preferences. Further lines of inquiry concern the pace, timing, and speed of exit decisions, or decisions to pursue venturing activities over time. Entrepreneurs' subjective perceptions of time, and their own and their stakeholders' orientations towards the short- vs. long-term, the past, present or future shape how they navigate entrepreneurship.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do objective dimensions such as duration, pace, timing, speed, and window of opportunity impact the entrepreneurship process?
  • How do they shape links between entrepreneurs' subjective time perspective, their biological time (chronotype), and cognitive processes related to information scanning and learning?
  • How do entrepreneurs' subjective time perspectives relate to their cognitions including information scanning and search, entrepreneurial learning, information associations and connections, and opportunity evaluation and judgment?
  • How do time perspectives relate to informal investors' and venture capitalists' decision to provide funding?
  • How do investors' time perspectives shape who they invest in, and the timing and size of their investments?
  • With what pace and speed do failure consequences vary with institutional and cultural contexts?
  • How does the timing of these consequences vary across groups of entrepreneurs including minoritized groups and differently abled entrepreneurs?
  • When and how does time perspective lead to unhealthy persistence in entrepreneurship and undermine well-being?
  • How do entrepreneurs' perception of time and the temporal development of the business impact venture emergence, business sustainability, and social entrepreneurship?
  • Do we see variations in temporal profiles and differences across industries and cultures?
  • How do the pacing of external events and entrepreneurs' own time perspective relate to how they manage equity, diversity, decolonization, and inclusion within their ventures?

Timeline

  • September 30, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
James Bort, DePaul University

Veroniek Collewaert, Vlerick Business School

Yuval Engel, University of Amsterdam

Evy Van Lancker, Ghent University

Johan Wiklund, Syracuse University

The startup workforce represents a distinct and consequential stakeholder in entrepreneurship that has been systematically understudied relative to founders and funders. Early insights from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies revealed how organizational changes within startups disproportionately impacted long-tenured employees. This pioneering work laid the foundation for understanding how startups differ from established firms in their approach to human capital, including fundamental aspects such as compensation, staffing, and performance management.

Contemporary research has deepened our understanding of the unique dynamics between startups and their employees. Whereas early research identified demographic patterns, illustrating that startup employees tend to be younger and risk-tolerant, recent work has uncovered more nuanced dynamics. For example, experienced employees often join startups when they have partners with stable careers, but can also command wage premiums as firms grow. Startup employees are drawn in by passionate founders, opportunities for greater freedom and responsibility, and the potential for significant financial upside.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Employee motivations and retention across venture stages
  • Recruitment, employer branding, and the role of prior affiliations in startup hiring
  • The influence of early employees on organizational culture, routines, and strategic direction
  • Compensation structures, equity arrangements, and evolving psychological contracts
  • Workforce well-being, occupational stress, and founder-employee emotional spillovers
  • The impact of hybrid and remote work on startup employment dynamics
  • The opportunities and adversity of AI in light of startup employment and work ethic, and workforce diversity, inclusion, and the role of HR professionalization in early-stage ventures
  • Worker voice, collective action, and power asymmetries in startups, including unionization, whistleblowing, hustle culture and exploitation, equity and vesting disputes, and the dark side of founder–employee relations
  • The regulatory and institutional environment of startup employment, including non-compete enforcement, worker classification, equity taxation, and visa regimes
  • Non-standard and hybrid labor forms, including contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost work, and globally distributed teams
  • Post-startup career trajectories, including employee mobility, alumni networks, and entrepreneurial spawning after exit, acquisition, or failure
  • The scaleup transition and its workforce implications, including when and how a startup workforce ceases to be one and how HR professionalization reshapes the employment relation
  • AI-native ventures as a new organizational form, where a small number of humans operate agentic systems and the category of workforce is itself reconstituted
  • Startup workforces outside North America and Western Europe, including emerging-economy, informal, and cross-border contexts

item.title: Les TPE : vers de nouveaux modèles d'affaires ?
item.content:encoded:
Marion Polge, Université de Montpellier

Isabelle Calmé, Université de Tours

Colette Fourcade, Université de Montpellier

Les très petites entreprises (TPE) restent largement sous-étudiées malgré leur importance statistique et sociale. Ce numéro interroge si elles constituent des organisations singulières au-delà de simples PME réduites. Par leur légèreté structurelle, leurs interactions intenses et leur proximité territoriale, elles développent des modes d'ajustement innovants et des dynamiques entrepreneuriales spécifiques, plus sobres et résilientes que les organisations plus établies.

Depuis 2020, les mutations systémiques – crises sanitaires, défis écologiques, numérisation – transforment profondément les TPE. Le numéro explore comment elles réinventent la performance au-delà de la croissance, adoptant des approches multiformes axées sur l'équilibre, la durabilité et l'impact local. Les nouvelles technologies créent tant des opportunités que des vulnérabilités pour ces organisations.

Appel publié par Revue internationale P M E Économie et gestion de la petite et moyenne entreprise. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Trajectoires stratégiques atypiques et diversification des profils de dirigeants de TPE : profils, motivations, rapport au travail et au risque, bifurcations de parcours
  • Redéfinition de la performance dans les TPE : indicateurs alternatifs, refus de la croissance, équilibre de vie, ancrage territorial, relations au vivant
  • TPE, écologie et raréfaction des ressources : modèles économiques frugaux, économie circulaire, décroissance choisie, entreprise régénérative, impact écologique
  • TPE et technologies : appropriation, marginalisation ou résistance face à la numérisation, à l'intelligence artificielle, à l'ubérisation ou à la plate-forme-économie
  • Formes alternatives d'organisation et d'innovation : bricolage, mutualisation, coopération, hybridation des statuts, pratiques informelles ou hybrides
  • Rôle des TPE dans les transitions sociales et territoriales : résilience locale, dynamiques d'inclusion, réponses aux crises systémiques, justice économique
  • Méthodologies et épistémologies de recherche adaptées aux TPE : recherches partenariales, approches critiques, récits de vie, ethnographie entrepreneuriale

Timeline

item.title: Novel Forms and Models of Organization
item.content:encoded:
Masatoshi Kato, Kwansei Gakuin University

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Roy Thurik, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Maksim Belitski, University of Reading

Alex Coad, Waseda Business School

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

Rapid technological change, globalization of supply chains and demand, increasing physical and digital connectivity, and inter-dependencies between actors in innovation and entrepreneurial ecosystems are forcing entrepreneurs and managers to rethink how they organize beyond the manufacturing of products and services, how they innovate, what technologies they adopt, and what markets they enter. The forms and models of organization affect a firm's ability to become exceptional. At the core of firm organization, the factors that distinguish them from their counterparts in the industry and region are firm size, firm age, stage of entrepreneurial continuum, institutional context, and technology-savviness. Firms that have been able to optimize their organization will outperform their regional competitors, markets, and industry; create new forms of growth at a different pace; and approach the innovation and production frontier. Through organizations in different forms, entrepreneurs and mature firms create product and process innovation and coordinate people, external ecosystem actors, government, suppliers, and capital to achieve frontier outcomes.

Appel publié par Journal of Small Business Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do firms adopting novel forms of organization differ in leadership, governance, and decision-making, and how do these differences shape innovation and productivity at the frontier?
  • What internal microstructures (e.g., boards, design, cross-functional teams, routines) enable firms to combine and recombine internal capabilities with external knowledge and ecosystem actors to achieve exceptional performance?
  • How do novel organizational forms affect authority, accountability, and coordination across functions, and what are the effects on innovation speed, product and managerial innovation, value creation, talent retention, growth, and scaling?
  • Which combinations of internal investment (make), external acquisition (buy), and alliance orchestration (ally) constitute novel organizational models that sustain frontier performance across firm types (hidden champions, niche leaders, sustained innovators, blitzscalers, scalers, etc.)?
  • How does the diversity (institutional and geographic) of external knowledge and innovation partners translate into firms adopting novel forms of organization, and what internal routines convert diverse inputs into outcomes?
  • Under what conditions do international vs regional knowledge collaboration and spillovers generate non-redundant knowledge that improves innovation and performance, and how do firms with different organizational forms apply, filter, and integrate this knowledge?
  • How does digitalization (AI and robotics, data systems, cloud, prominent role of intangibles, etc.) reshape internal process architectures, and which organizational forms best convert digital investments into productivity and innovation gains?
  • Which governance models (data rights, intellectual property, cybersecurity, partner contracts) enable novel organizational forms to adopt and scale complex technologies while maintaining trust and control in technology and partners?
  • How do digitally savvy firms pivot and reconfigure organizational forms to build resilience to supply, demand, and geopolitical shocks, and what design features predict faster recovery and sustained innovation?
  • How do firms implement novel forms of organization while embedded in industry and entrepreneurial ecosystems, and how does ecosystem position shape organizational models for innovation and scaling?
  • How do niche leaders and other exceptional performers orchestrate global supply chains as an organizational capability, not only a sourcing choice, across regional and international contexts?
  • What partner portfolio mixes (universities, suppliers, customers, competitors, government, research labs, conferences, competitions, trade and industrial associations, scientific communities) are associated with frontier outcomes, and what form of organization do firms need to adopt to efficiently govern such collaborations, knowledge spillovers, and firm strategies?
  • How do relationships with government shape novel organizational models through procurement, standards, subsidies, and cluster governance, and when do these relationships enhance versus constrain innovation and productivity?
  • How do organizational models vary between emerging and traditional industries and across industrial clusters of novel and emerging industries where traditional forms of organization are no longer working?
  • How do deglobalization pressures and techno-nationalism reshape firms' organizational choices?
  • What distinctive business model configurations characterize exceptional performers across countries, regions, industries, and stages of growth, age, and size, and how are these configurations enabled by organizational form?
  • How do European, Asian, American, and African leaders in WEIRD and non-WEIRD countries differ in adopting and experimenting with novel forms of organization?
  • What contextual factors explain these cross-country differences?
  • Do niche leaders exhibit distinctive innovation patterns (radical vs incremental, product vs process, ecosystem vs standalone), and which organizational designs best explain variation in these patterns and their performance effects?

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Manuscript submission opens
  • November 15, 2026: Submission deadline for extended abstracts and full papers
  • January 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Ethics and Entrepreneurship: Foundations and Philosophical Perspectives
item.content:encoded:
Tina Dacin, Wilfrid Laurier University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Jean Clarke, Emlyon Business School

Jaco Lok, Macquarie University

Max Ganzin, Macquarie University

This special issue examines the ethical foundations of entrepreneurship, positioning ethics as central to entrepreneurial practice rather than a constraint on it. The issue brings together entrepreneurship studies and philosophical ethics to explore how venture creation, opportunity recognition, and stakeholder engagement involve fundamental questions about responsibility, justice, and human flourishing. It investigates the tension between entrepreneurship's capacity for creativity and disruption and concerns about commodification and self-optimization.

The special issue welcomes diverse methodological and disciplinary perspectives examining how philosophical traditions such as virtue ethics, phenomenology, pragmatism, and deontology illuminate entrepreneurial practice. It particularly emphasizes entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty and fluidity, where ethical judgment must balance competing stakeholder interests without reliance on established protocols. The issue seeks papers exploring how entrepreneurship and ethics can deepen each other's understanding through examining contingency, creativity, authenticity, care, and emerging futures.

Appel publié par Journal of Business Ethics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Philosophical dimensions of ethics and how different philosophical traditions inform understanding of entrepreneurship as an ethical practice
  • Phenomenology of the entrepreneurial experience, uncertainty, autonomy, and decision-making
  • The entrepreneur and ethical subjectivity, agency, embodiment, and identity
  • Ethics and rule-breaking in entrepreneurial contexts
  • Stakeholder relations, trust-building, and ethical objectives
  • Whether entrepreneurship is inherently ethical or exploitative
  • Entrepreneurship and technological mediation in the digital age
  • Ethics, value, and the framing of entrepreneurial goals and opportunities
  • Temporal dimensions of entrepreneurial ethics and long-term considerations

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Entrepreneurship and the Creation of Decent Work for All
item.content:encoded:
Societal changes, environment, political and financial crises inevitably affect labor markets and the quality of employment. Recent pandemic and global political changes have only demonstrated how quickly one's employment and workplace situation can change. Among other factors, entrepreneurship could play a crucial role in the creation of decent work, especially in a volatile environment.

Understanding the relationship between entrepreneurship and working conditions is crucial for supporting policies and instruments which aim at more productive, decent work, fair wages, better access to the labor market, and improved job opportunities for all.

In order to fully represent this multifaceted topic, we would like to gather a spectrum of current perspectives in a single Collection, facilitating a better understanding of possibilities and ways of striving toward the goal of 'achieving full and productive employment and decent work for all' (SDG 8 of the U.N.).

Appel publié par International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Technology Transfer through Collaboration: Bridging Academia, Policy, and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Maksim Belitski, Loyola University New Orleans

James Cunningham, Newcastle University

Riccardo Fini, University of Bologna

Simon Mosey, University of Nottingham

Phillip H. Phan, Johns Hopkins University

This special collection seeks submissions that investigate technology transfer, entrepreneurship, and innovation through partnerships between academic researchers and external stakeholders such as practitioners and policymakers. The editors recognize that meaningful research in this field often benefits from close collaboration across disciplinary and sectoral boundaries, providing access to emerging phenomena and underexplored mechanisms that traditional approaches might miss.

The collection particularly welcomes papers co-authored by academics and non-academic partners including technology transfer professionals, policymakers, entrepreneurs, investors, and innovation intermediaries. Such collaborative work is expected to generate unique insights, improve data access, broaden empirical scope, and tackle fundamental questions from diverse perspectives while maintaining rigorous academic standards.

Appel publié par The Journal of Technology Transfer. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Technology transfer and collaborations between academic researchers and non-academic actors
  • Entrepreneurship and innovation emerging from academic-practitioner-policymaker interactions
  • Co-authored research involving academics and technology transfer professionals, policymakers, entrepreneurs, innovators, investors, industry experts, platform managers, R&D managers, or innovation intermediaries
  • Development of new theory through collaborative engagement
  • Enrichment of empirical analysis using collaborative perspectives
  • Access to distinctive data through academic-non-academic partnerships
  • Research combining methodological rigor with practical and policy-relevant insights

item.title: From Shallow Waters to Deep Dives: Indigenous Theorizing on Chinese Family Enterprises
item.content:encoded:
Bingbing Ge, Lancaster University Management School

Hanqing Fang, Missouri University of Science and Technology

Alfredo De Massis, D'Annunzio University of Chieti-Pescara

Junsheng Dou, Zhejiang University

Winnie Qian Peng, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

This Special Issue aims to advance theoretical and empirical discussions on Chinese family businesses and entrepreneurial families by diving deep into them as contexts that challenge prevailing Western theories and as generative contexts for indigenous theorizing in family entrepreneurship. Scholarship has increasingly highlighted the importance of context in shaping entrepreneurial phenomena and emphasized entrepreneurship as a socially constructed process. Yet dominant frameworks in family business and family entrepreneurship—such as socioemotional wealth (SEW), agency theory, stewardship, and the resource-based view (RBV)—were largely developed in Western institutional and cultural environments characterized by individualism, contractual governance, and relatively liberal market economies. When these frameworks are applied to Chinese family enterprises, their underlying assumptions about self-interest, agency costs, governance logics, and resource valuation often prove misaligned, producing puzzling or contradictory findings.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Indigenous Theorizing and Concept Development: Building indigenous theories rooted in Chinese cultural, institutional, and geopolitical conditions, drawing from Confucian ethics, guanxi logics, or dynastic continuity as explanatory mechanisms
  • Entrepreneurship as Constraint and Renewal: Exploring how institutional and cultural elements such as filial obligation, demographic legacies, and social perceptions shape entrepreneurial succession
  • History-informed research: Taking a history-informed perspective to understand entrepreneurship and family business practices, including innovation through tradition
  • Regional Heterogeneity: Incorporating regional institutional heterogeneity as a central explanatory factor in family entrepreneurship across China's varied development models and cultural norms
  • Purpose in Chinese Business Families: Theorizing Chinese family offices and their approaches to transgenerational wealth through multi-enterprise portfolios and informal arrangements
  • Gender and Patriarchal Paradoxes: Theorizing gendered pathways of leadership specific to the Chinese context and female successors' roles in patriarchal traditions
  • Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG), Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Communal Orientation: Understanding how cultural embeddedness shapes responsibility, CSR, and legitimacy in Chinese family firms
  • Geopolitical Turbulence as Institutional Hybridity: Theorizing how family firms navigate global turbulence under conditions of institutional hybridity and restricted learning opportunities

item.title: Parenthood and Entrepreneurship: A New Research Agenda
item.content:encoded:
Shuang Lu Frost, Aarhus University

Magdalena Markowska, King's College London

Kai Roland Green, Aarhus University

Kimberly Eddleston, Northeastern University

Alisa Jno-Charles, Babson College

Haibo Zhou, University of Nottingham Ningbo China

Ulla Hytti, University of Turku

According to the 2021 Global Entrepreneurship Monitor report, nearly half of early-stage entrepreneurs globally are raising children. These parent-entrepreneurs navigate a unique landscape where the demands of child-rearing directly intersect with the pressures of business creation and survival at the individual, family, business, and societal levels. The quest for work-family balance draws many entrepreneurs. Yet entrepreneurship often intensifies the work-family conflict it was meant to resolve, affecting both business performance and personal well-being. Motherhood and fatherhood thus play a critical yet underexplored role in shaping entrepreneurial motivations, practices, and outcomes. Understanding these dynamics is vital for entrepreneurial practice: it can inform the design of more effective support systems and guide policymakers in creating inclusive ecosystems that recognise the dual roles many founders play.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do parent-entrepreneurs negotiate entrepreneurial and parental identities across gender, culture, and sexuality?
  • How do emerging models of fatherhood/motherhood shape entrepreneurship?
  • What role does founder identity transformation play in the transition to entrepreneurial parenthood?
  • How do single parents, LGBTQ+ parents, and individuals in non-normative family forms experience entrepreneurial entry and growth?
  • How is role conflict or role enrichment experienced differently by mothers and fathers in entrepreneurial families?
  • How do partner dynamics and household egalitarianism shape entrepreneurial decisions?
  • What specific resources (cognitive, financial, human, social capital) are transmitted from entrepreneurial parents to children?
  • What are the lived experiences and well-being outcomes of children growing up in entrepreneurial households?
  • How do macro-level factors (e.g., economic instability, policy frameworks) interact with household dynamics to influence children's outcomes and orientations?
  • In what ways do interparental interactions and household role negotiations shape children's perception of entrepreneurship?
  • How do entrepreneurial households balance opportunity creation with potential stress or instability for children?
  • How do regional policies, parental leave systems, and childcare infrastructure shape entrepreneurial entry, continuation, and exit among parents?
  • How do parent-entrepreneurs' experiences differ across welfare regimes (liberal, social-democratic, conservative, developing-country contexts)?
  • What role do informal institutions and extended family networks play in enabling or constraining parental entrepreneurship?
  • How does the portrayal of parent-entrepreneurs in media, public discourse, and cultural narratives affect entrepreneurial motives and sources of satisfaction?
  • How does the self-representation and identity work of parent-entrepreneurs on social media and in entrepreneurial communities contribute to their business success and well-being?
  • How do discursive ideals of 'good motherhood' or 'involved fatherhood' constrain or enable entrepreneurial action?
  • What are the longitudinal effects of entrepreneurship on family well-being, and vice versa?
  • How does parenthood influence innovation, creativity, or business performance?
  • How do entrepreneurial career trajectories differ based on family status, parenting roles, and the timing of parenthood relative to venture creation?

Timeline

  • June 1, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • July 1, 2027: Manuscript deadline
